topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A broker operates as a sole proprietor with no separate corporate or LLC entity. If the brokerage is sued and loses a judgment exceeding its business assets, what happens to the broker's personal, non-business assets?
choice_a: They remain exposed -- a sole proprietor has unlimited personal liability for business obligations, because no legal separation exists between the individual and the business
choice_b: They are always fully protected, because New York treats every real estate business as a separate legal entity regardless of its actual structure
choice_c: They are protected only if the broker purchased general liability insurance
choice_d: They are protected automatically once the broker obtains a DOS business-name approval
explanation: A sole proprietorship creates no legal separation between the individual and the business -- the owner has unlimited personal liability, meaning personal assets (beyond the business itself) can be reached to satisfy business debts or judgments, which is the central tradeoff against choosing a liability-shielding structure like an LLC or corporation.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general business-entity liability principle (sole proprietorship unlimited personal liability), as applied to a real estate brokerage

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Two individuals operate a real estate brokerage together as a general partnership, with no LLC or corporate structure. If one partner commits negligence within the scope of the partnership's business, what is the general liability exposure of the other, non-negligent partner?
choice_a: The other partner can be held jointly and severally liable, since general partners are each personally liable for partnership obligations arising from a partner's conduct within the scope of the business
choice_b: The other partner has no liability exposure whatsoever, since only the negligent partner personally can ever be sued
choice_c: Liability can only be imposed on the partnership's bank account, never on either individual partner personally
choice_d: The other partner's liability is automatically capped at the amount of their original capital contribution
explanation: In a general partnership, partners are jointly and severally personally liable for partnership obligations and for a co-partner's wrongful conduct occurring within the scope of the partnership's business -- a structural risk that distinguishes a general partnership from an LLC or corporation, where owners generally are not personally liable for the entity's obligations merely by virtue of ownership.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated New York general partnership liability principle (joint and several liability), as applied to a real estate brokerage

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Must a general partnership formally register or file organizational documents with New York State in order to legally exist as a partnership?
choice_a: No -- a general partnership can arise simply from the parties' agreement (written or verbal) or conduct to carry on a business as co-owners for profit, without any state filing being required for the partnership itself to exist
choice_b: Yes -- a general partnership does not legally exist in New York until Articles of Partnership are filed with and approved by DOS
choice_c: Yes -- a general partnership requires the same certificate of formation filing as an LLC before it can conduct any business
choice_d: No -- but only if all partners are already individually licensed real estate brokers
explanation: Unlike corporations and LLCs, a general partnership is not created by a state filing -- it can arise from the parties' agreement or conduct to carry on a business as co-owners for profit, which is one reason general partnerships are considered simple to form but comparatively risky given the unlimited personal liability each partner bears.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general partnership formation principle (no state filing required to exist), distinct from RPL Section 440-a's separate licensing requirement for the entity's brokerage activity

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage is organized as a limited liability company (LLC) whose members are the individual licensees who own the business. If the LLC itself is sued over a business debt, what is the general liability exposure of an individual member simply by virtue of being an LLC member?
choice_a: Generally, the member is not personally liable for the LLC's debts or obligations solely by reason of being a member -- the LLC's own assets, not the member's personal assets, are the general target for satisfying the entity's obligations
choice_b: Each member is automatically personally liable for the full amount of every LLC debt, identical to a sole proprietor
choice_c: Liability is imposed at random by DOS on whichever member happens to be the designated broker of record
choice_d: LLC members can never be held personally liable under any circumstances, even where they have personally guaranteed a debt or committed fraud
explanation: A core feature of the LLC structure is that a member is generally not personally liable for the entity's debts and obligations solely because of their membership status -- unlike a general partner or sole proprietor -- though this limited-liability shield is not absolute, as it can be lost through personal guarantees, personal wrongdoing, or a successful veil-piercing claim.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated LLC limited-liability principle, as applied to a real estate brokerage entity

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under New York's 'piercing the corporate veil' doctrine, what must a plaintiff generally prove to hold an LLC's or corporation's owner personally liable for the entity's obligations, despite the entity's normal liability shield?
choice_a: That the owner exercised complete domination over the entity with respect to the transaction at issue, and used that domination to commit a fraud or wrong against the plaintiff that caused the plaintiff's injury
choice_b: Simply that the entity is a small, closely held business with only one or two owners
choice_c: Simply that the entity failed to turn a profit in its first year of operation
choice_d: That the entity's name includes the word 'LLC' or 'Inc.' rather than a fully spelled-out business designation
explanation: New York courts apply a two-part veil-piercing test, requiring proof that the owner exercised complete domination of the entity in respect to the transaction attacked, and that this domination was used to commit a fraud or wrong against the plaintiff resulting in injury -- mere single or closely held ownership, by itself, is not enough to disregard the entity's separate legal existence.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated New York veil-piercing doctrine (domination-plus-wrong test), as applied to a real estate business entity

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Which of the following is most likely to support a claim to pierce the corporate veil of a real estate brokerage's LLC or corporation?
choice_a: The owner routinely commingles personal funds with the business's accounts and withdraws business funds for personal use once a claim against the business arises, leaving the entity unable to satisfy a judgment
choice_b: The owner maintains separate business bank accounts, keeps adequate capitalization for the business's operations, and follows corporate formalities like keeping business records distinct from personal ones
choice_c: The entity has been profitable and adequately capitalized every year since formation
choice_d: The entity's broker of record holds continuing education credits current with DOS requirements
explanation: Commingling personal and business funds, undercapitalization, and diverting assets out of the entity (especially once a claim arises, leaving the entity judgment-proof) are treated as strong indicators supporting veil-piercing, because they show the entity was operated as the owner's personal instrumentality rather than as a genuinely separate legal person -- in contrast, maintaining formalities and adequate capitalization is exactly what preserves the liability shield.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated New York veil-piercing risk-factor doctrine (commingling, undercapitalization, asset diversion)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A real estate brokerage organized as a C corporation earns net profit and distributes a portion of it to its shareholders as dividends. How is that profit generally taxed?
choice_a: Twice -- once as income to the corporation itself, and again as income to the shareholders when the after-tax profit is distributed to them as dividends
choice_b: Only once, at the corporate level, with no further tax owed by the shareholders when dividends are received
choice_c: Only once, at the shareholder level, with the corporation itself owing no tax on its profits
choice_d: Not at all -- real estate brokerage income is categorically exempt from both corporate and individual income tax
explanation: A defining feature of the traditional C corporation is 'double taxation': the corporation pays tax on its own net profits, and then shareholders separately pay individual income tax on dividends distributed from those already-taxed profits -- a structural cost that leads many small real estate brokerages to consider a pass-through structure instead.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal business-taxation principle (C corporation double taxation), as applied to a real estate brokerage

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage organized as an LLC (taxed by default as a partnership/disregarded entity) or as an S corporation generally avoids the 'double taxation' that applies to a C corporation because:
choice_a: Business profits generally pass through directly to the owners' individual tax returns and are taxed only once, at the owner level, rather than being taxed separately at the entity level and again when distributed
choice_b: Such entities are entirely exempt from federal income tax under all circumstances
choice_c: Only the entity itself pays tax, and the owners never report any of the business income on their personal returns
choice_d: New York State grants real estate brokerages an automatic tax exemption regardless of entity type
explanation: LLCs (by default) and S corporations are generally 'pass-through' entities: business income, gains, and losses flow through to the owners' individual tax returns and are taxed once, at the owner level -- avoiding the separate entity-level tax that applies to C corporation profits, which is a major reason many small real estate brokerages choose an LLC or S corporation structure.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal pass-through taxation principle (LLC/S corporation default treatment)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under New York Limited Liability Company Law Section 206, beyond filing Articles of Organization, what additional formation step is a newly formed New York LLC (such as a brokerage LLC) generally required to complete?
choice_a: Publishing a copy of the articles (or a notice of their substance) once a week for six successive weeks in two newspapers designated by the county clerk, then filing a certificate of publication with DOS
choice_b: Nothing further -- Articles of Organization alone are always sufficient to complete LLC formation with no other required step
choice_c: Obtaining sign-off from every competing brokerage in the same county
choice_d: Publishing the articles in a single national newspaper of the LLC's choosing, one time only
explanation: LLC Law Section 206 imposes a distinctively New York publication requirement: within 120 days of formation, the LLC must publish a copy of its articles (or a notice of their substance) once a week for six successive weeks in two newspapers designated by the county clerk of the county where its office is located, then file a certificate of publication -- failure to do so suspends the LLC's authority to conduct business in New York.
source_note: New York Limited Liability Company Law Section 206 (Affidavits of Publication)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: If a brokerage's LLC fails to timely complete the publication requirement and file the resulting certificate of publication with DOS within 120 days of formation, what is the general consequence?
choice_a: The LLC's authority to carry on, conduct, or transact business in New York is suspended until the requirement is satisfied
choice_b: Nothing -- the publication requirement carries no enforcement consequence of any kind
choice_c: The LLC is automatically and permanently dissolved with no opportunity to cure the defect
choice_d: Every individual member automatically loses their real estate license
explanation: LLC Law Section 206 provides that if proof of publication is not filed with the Department of State within 120 days after formation, the LLC's authority to carry on, conduct, or transact business in New York is suspended -- a consequence distinct from (and in addition to) the separate real-estate-specific licensing requirements imposed on the entity under RPL Section 440-a.
source_note: New York Limited Liability Company Law Section 206 (Affidavits of Publication -- consequence of noncompliance)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage is organized as a corporation with a board of directors and corporate officers. Separate from any real estate agency duties those individuals may owe to clients, what general fiduciary duties do corporate officers and directors owe to the corporation itself?
choice_a: The duty of care (acting with the diligence and prudence an ordinarily careful person would exercise in a like position) and the duty of loyalty (putting the corporation's interests ahead of the officer's or director's own personal interests)
choice_b: No fiduciary duties at all -- officers and directors owe legal obligations only to their individual real estate clients, never to the corporation itself
choice_c: Only a duty to maximize the officer's own personal compensation
choice_d: Only a duty to attend a minimum number of board meetings per year, with no substantive duty of care or loyalty
explanation: Corporate officers and directors owe fiduciary duties of care and loyalty to the corporation itself -- a distinct layer of obligation from any agency-based fiduciary duty a broker or salesperson separately owes to a real estate client -- requiring good-faith, diligent decision-making in the corporation's best interest and prohibiting self-dealing that favors the officer's or director's own interests over the corporation's.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general corporate-governance fiduciary duty doctrine (duty of care and duty of loyalty), applied to a real estate brokerage organized as a corporation

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: The 'business judgment rule' generally protects a corporate director's or officer's decision from being second-guessed by a court, but this protection typically does NOT extend to a decision that:
choice_a: Involved a disabling conflict of interest, was made in bad faith, or was made without the director or officer first becoming reasonably informed
choice_b: Turned out, with hindsight, to have been financially unsuccessful for the corporation
choice_c: Was made unanimously by the full board of directors
choice_d: Involved real property rather than personal property
explanation: The business judgment rule presumes directors and officers acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the corporation's best interest -- but that presumption does not shield a decision tainted by a disabling conflict of interest, bad faith, or a failure to become reasonably informed before acting, even though the rule generally does not punish a good-faith decision merely because it turned out badly in hindsight.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general corporate-governance business judgment rule doctrine

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Two competing, unaffiliated brokerages agree between themselves that neither will accept referrals from or cooperate on transactions with a third, discount brokerage in their market, specifically to pressure it out of business. What antitrust concept does this best illustrate?
choice_a: A group boycott (concerted refusal to deal) -- an agreement among competitors to collectively withhold business from a targeted competitor, which is treated as a serious antitrust violation under the Sherman Act
choice_b: A lawful, routine business decision that raises no antitrust concern because each brokerage is simply choosing its own trading partners
choice_c: A violation of New York's fair housing law rather than of any antitrust law
choice_d: This is legal as long as the two brokerages document their reasons for excluding the third brokerage in writing
explanation: A group boycott -- two or more competitors agreeing to collectively refuse to deal with or refer business to a targeted competitor -- is a distinct form of Sherman Act violation from price-fixing or tying, generally treated as a serious antitrust concern because it uses coordinated action among competitors to disadvantage or exclude a rival, rather than each firm independently deciding whom to do business with.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal antitrust principle (Sherman Act Section 1 group boycott/concerted refusal to deal), applied to real estate brokerage competition

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A single brokerage, acting entirely on its own and without consulting any competing brokerage, decides internally to stop referring clients to a particular title company it no longer trusts. Does this unilateral decision, by itself, violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act?
choice_a: No -- Section 1 requires a contract, combination, or conspiracy between two or more separate parties; a single firm's independent, unilateral business decision does not, by itself, satisfy that concerted-action requirement
choice_b: Yes -- any decision by any brokerage to stop working with any other business automatically violates the Sherman Act
choice_c: Yes, but only if the brokerage is the largest firm in its local market
choice_d: No, but only because title companies are entirely exempt from antitrust law
explanation: Section 1 of the Sherman Act reaches concerted action -- a contract, combination, or conspiracy between two or more separate economic actors -- so a single brokerage's unilateral decision, made independently without an agreement with a competitor, does not by itself establish a Section 1 violation, which is the key distinction between lawful independent business judgment and unlawful coordinated conduct like price-fixing or a group boycott.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal antitrust principle (Sherman Act Section 1 concerted-action requirement), applied to real estate brokerage practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Separate from the federal Sherman Act, New York has its own state-level antitrust statute found in General Business Law Sections 340-347. What is this statute commonly called?
choice_a: The Donnelly Act, often described as New York's 'Little Sherman Act'
choice_b: The Martin Act
choice_c: The Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law
choice_d: The Uniform Commercial Code
explanation: New York's Donnelly Act (General Business Law Sections 340-347), enacted in 1899 and commonly called New York's 'Little Sherman Act,' prohibits price-fixing, bid-rigging, territorial and customer allocation, monopolization, boycotts, and tying arrangements -- providing a state-law antitrust enforcement mechanism that runs parallel to the federal Sherman Act, distinct from the Martin Act's separate securities/investment-fraud focus.
source_note: General Business Law Article 22, Sections 340-347 (Donnelly Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under the Donnelly Act, in addition to civil enforcement by the New York Attorney General, what other enforcement avenue is available for a violation such as price-fixing among competing brokerages?
choice_a: Both criminal prosecution (a felony) and a private civil lawsuit by an injured party seeking treble (triple) damages
choice_b: No enforcement mechanism exists beyond a non-binding letter of reprimand from DOS
choice_c: Only a private lawsuit is available; the Attorney General has no authority to bring any Donnelly Act action
choice_d: Only DOS may bring a Donnelly Act case, through the same license-discipline process used for RPL Article 12-A violations
explanation: A Donnelly Act violation carries multiple layers of exposure: it is a felony (criminal fine and, for individuals, potential imprisonment), the Attorney General may bring a civil enforcement action for substantial fines, and a private party injured by the violation (such as a brokerage harmed by a competitors' price-fixing scheme) may sue for treble damages -- a materially different and more severe enforcement structure than DOS's separate license-discipline authority under RPL Article 12-A.
source_note: General Business Law Article 22 (Donnelly Act) -- criminal, civil, and private treble-damages enforcement

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under Sherman Act doctrine, a horizontal price-fixing agreement among competing brokerages is treated as a 'per se' violation. What does that classification mean for how a court analyzes the agreement?
choice_a: The agreement is treated as automatically illegal without requiring proof of its actual effect on competition or any inquiry into a business justification, because the conduct is considered so inherently harmful that further analysis is unnecessary
choice_b: The agreement is presumptively legal unless a competitor can prove specific dollar-figure harm
choice_c: 'Per se' means the agreement is evaluated only under New York state law, never under federal law
choice_d: 'Per se' means the agreement is illegal only if it lasted longer than one calendar year
explanation: A 'per se' antitrust violation -- the category that includes horizontal price-fixing, bid-rigging, and market/customer allocation -- is treated as automatically unlawful without a detailed inquiry into its actual competitive effects or any claimed business justification, in contrast to conduct analyzed under the more fact-intensive 'rule of reason,' which asks whether a restraint unreasonably harms competition under the specific circumstances.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal antitrust doctrine (per se rule vs. rule of reason), applied to horizontal price-fixing among competing brokerages

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Several competing brokerages in a region agree amongst themselves to each operate exclusively in separate, non-overlapping territories and to refrain from soliciting listings in each other's assigned area. What antitrust problem does this create, distinct from price-fixing or a group boycott?
choice_a: A market/territorial allocation agreement -- competitors dividing up markets or customers between themselves, which (like price-fixing) is treated as a per se antitrust violation because it eliminates competition between the agreeing firms
choice_b: No antitrust problem exists, because each brokerage remains free to set its own commission rates within its assigned territory
choice_c: This is only a concern if the agreement is formalized in a signed written contract; an informal understanding would be entirely lawful
choice_d: This is a fair housing violation, not an antitrust matter, because it involves geographic areas
explanation: An agreement among competitors to divide up territories or customers -- even without any explicit price term -- is its own distinct category of horizontal antitrust violation (market/territorial allocation), analyzed as a per se violation because it directly eliminates the competition between the agreeing firms that antitrust law is designed to protect, regardless of whether the agreement is written or informal.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal antitrust principle (horizontal market/territorial allocation), applied to real estate brokerage competition

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Following the 2024 national settlement of major buyer-broker commission antitrust litigation against the National Association of REALTORS, one of the central practice changes adopted industry-wide was:
choice_a: Prohibiting the inclusion of buyer-broker compensation offers on Multiple Listing Service (MLS) listings
choice_b: Making MLS participation entirely voluntary for the first time
choice_c: Eliminating the requirement that any purchase contract be in writing
choice_d: Setting a uniform, fixed national commission rate of 5% for every transaction
explanation: A central conduct-change term of the 2024 nationwide antitrust settlement (arising from litigation alleging that requiring sellers to offer buyer-broker compensation via the MLS suppressed price competition among buyer brokers) was prohibiting the display of buyer-broker compensation offers on MLS listings -- compensation could no longer be advertised through that centralized channel, though brokerages remain free to negotiate compensation directly.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated 2024 NAR nationwide antitrust commission settlement summary (Burnett/Sitzer-Burnett litigation and related settlement terms)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under the practice changes adopted following the 2024 NAR commission-litigation settlement, what must generally happen before a buyer's broker shows homes to a prospective buyer client?
choice_a: The buyer and the buyer's broker must enter into a written agreement specifying the broker's compensation, before the broker tours homes with that buyer
choice_b: Nothing new is required; the settlement made no changes to how buyer representation may begin
choice_c: The seller must personally approve the buyer's choice of broker in writing
choice_d: The buyer's broker must first obtain a separate federal antitrust compliance license
explanation: Alongside barring buyer-broker compensation offers from MLS listings, the 2024 settlement's conduct terms required prospective buyers and their brokers to enter into a written buyer-representation agreement -- specifying compensation terms -- before the broker begins showing homes, formalizing and front-loading a disclosure that industry practice had previously handled less consistently.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated 2024 NAR nationwide antitrust commission settlement summary (written buyer-agreement requirement)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A regional multiple listing service, controlled by its member brokerages, votes to categorically deny membership to any brokerage that advertises a reduced or 'discount' commission structure. What antitrust theory would most directly apply to challenge this practice?
choice_a: A group boycott/concerted refusal to deal -- the MLS's competing member-brokerages are collectively agreeing, through the MLS's governance structure, to exclude a category of competitor based on its pricing model
choice_b: No antitrust theory would apply, since MLS organizations are entirely exempt from all antitrust laws
choice_c: This is purely a contract dispute with no antitrust dimension whatsoever
choice_d: This can only be challenged under the federal Fair Housing Act, not under any antitrust statute
explanation: Because an MLS is typically controlled by competing member brokerages acting collectively, a decision to categorically exclude brokerages based on their commission-pricing model implicates group-boycott/concerted-refusal-to-deal antitrust theory -- MLS organizations are not categorically exempt from antitrust scrutiny, and using MLS governance to disadvantage lower-cost competitors has been a recurring focus of both government and private antitrust litigation in the real estate industry.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal antitrust principle (group boycott via MLS governance), applied to real estate brokerage competition

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A listing broker, without disclosing it to the seller, arranges to purchase the seller's own listed property personally through an LLC the broker secretly controls, at a price below what other buyers were offering. What is the primary ethical/legal problem with this arrangement?
choice_a: Undisclosed self-dealing -- using an entity structure to conceal the broker's own beneficial interest as a purchaser creates an undisclosed conflict of interest and can constitute a breach of the broker's duty of honesty and full disclosure to the seller, regardless of how the purchasing entity is titled
choice_b: There is no problem, since forming an LLC to purchase property is always a lawful, routine business transaction with no disclosure implications
choice_c: The only issue is that the broker did not personally sign the purchase contract using their own name
choice_d: This is only a concern if the LLC purchasing the property was formed outside New York State
explanation: While forming and using a business entity to purchase property is ordinarily lawful, concealing a broker's own beneficial ownership behind that entity while simultaneously representing the seller in the same transaction is undisclosed self-dealing -- a serious conflict of interest that can expose the broker to discipline for untrustworthy conduct and civil liability, entirely independent of whether the purchasing entity itself was properly formed.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated business-ethics/conflict-of-interest principle (undisclosed self-dealing through a controlled entity), applied to real estate brokerage practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: After a broker's representation of a former client has fully ended and the transaction has closed, does the broker's ethical duty to keep that former client's confidential information confidential also end?
choice_a: No -- the general ethical obligation to protect a client's confidential information (such as their financial circumstances or negotiating position) is understood to survive the end of the brokerage relationship itself, not merely to apply while the relationship is active
choice_b: Yes -- once a transaction closes, a broker is free to disclose or use anything learned about the former client for the broker's own future advantage
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial clients, never for residential clients
choice_d: This obligation has never been recognized in any professional or business ethics context
explanation: Consistent with broader professional and business ethics doctrine, the duty to safeguard a client's confidential information is generally understood to continue beyond the formal end of the representation -- a former client's sensitive financial or negotiating information should not be disclosed or exploited simply because the underlying transaction has closed and the agency relationship has ended.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general professional/business ethics confidentiality principle, applied to a former real estate client relationship

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A listing broker represents only the seller in a transaction and owes the seller (not the unrepresented buyer) fiduciary duties of loyalty and confidentiality. Does this mean the broker has no ethical obligations at all toward the unrepresented buyer, as a customer rather than a client?
choice_a: No -- even absent a fiduciary relationship, a broker generally still owes a customer basic obligations of honesty and fair dealing, such as not making false statements about the property, distinct from (and lesser than) the full fiduciary duties owed to the broker's own client
choice_b: Yes -- a broker may say anything at all to an unrepresented customer, including knowingly false statements, since no fiduciary relationship exists
choice_c: Yes -- ethical obligations only exist between a broker and their own directly compensating client, with no obligations running to any other party in the transaction
choice_d: No -- the broker actually owes the unrepresented buyer the exact same full fiduciary duties owed to the seller
explanation: General business/professional ethics doctrine distinguishes the full fiduciary duties (loyalty, confidentiality, undivided allegiance) a broker owes their own client from the narrower baseline obligations of honesty and fair dealing owed to a customer on the other side of the transaction -- a broker without an agency relationship to a party still may not lie to or deliberately mislead that party, even though the broker is not acting as that party's advocate.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general business ethics distinction between fiduciary-client obligations and baseline customer honesty/fair-dealing obligations

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What are the basic elements of a claim for tortious interference with an existing contract, as generally applied in a business context?
choice_a: A valid contract between two parties, the defendant's knowledge of that contract, the defendant's intentional and improper procurement of its breach, and resulting damages
choice_b: Simply that the defendant is a competitor of one of the contracting parties, with no further showing required
choice_c: Proof that the contract in question was required to be in writing under the statute of frauds
choice_d: Proof that the defendant personally profited from the breach, which is the only element that must be shown
explanation: A tortious interference with contract claim generally requires: (1) the existence of a valid contract between the plaintiff and a third party, (2) the defendant's knowledge of that contract, (3) the defendant's intentional procurement of the third party's breach without justification, and (4) resulting damages -- a distinct business tort from a breach-of-contract claim itself, since it targets a third party who caused the breach rather than the breaching party.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general business-tort doctrine (tortious interference with contract elements), applied to a real estate business context

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: How does a claim for tortious interference with 'prospective business relations' (or prospective economic advantage) generally differ from tortious interference with an existing contract?
choice_a: It applies where no contract has yet been formed -- protecting a party's reasonable expectation of a future business relationship or economic benefit from wrongful third-party interference, rather than protecting an already-existing contractual right
choice_b: It is legally identical in every respect to interference with an existing contract, with no meaningful distinction
choice_c: It applies only to relationships between family members, never to business relationships
choice_d: It requires proof of a written, signed agreement, exactly like a claim for interference with an existing contract
explanation: Interference with prospective business relations protects a party's reasonable expectation of a future economic benefit -- such as a likely upcoming listing or referral -- from wrongful third-party interference, even though no binding contract yet exists, whereas interference with an existing contract requires an already-formed, valid contractual relationship that the defendant caused to be breached.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general business-tort doctrine (interference with prospective business relations vs. interference with an existing contract)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A seller has already signed an exclusive right-to-sell listing agreement with Brokerage A. A salesperson from Brokerage B, knowing about the existing exclusive listing, persuades the seller to breach that agreement early and sign a new listing with Brokerage B instead. Does this conduct raise a tortious interference concern?
choice_a: Yes -- intentionally inducing a party to breach an existing, known contract (here, the exclusive listing agreement with Brokerage A) can constitute tortious interference with contract, exposing Brokerage B to liability separate from any dispute between the seller and Brokerage A
choice_b: No -- competing for a client's business is always completely lawful no matter what existing agreements the client has already signed
choice_c: No -- tortious interference can never apply to real estate listing agreements under any circumstances
choice_d: This is only a licensing-law violation, with absolutely no possible civil tort exposure
explanation: The key distinction is between lawful competition for a prospective client (soliciting someone who is not yet bound to a competitor) and unlawfully inducing a party to breach an existing, known contract -- Brokerage B's knowing inducement of the seller's breach of the exclusive listing with Brokerage A can expose Brokerage B to tortious interference liability, on top of whatever contractual dispute the seller now has with Brokerage A.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated business-tort doctrine (tortious interference with an existing exclusive listing agreement), applied to competing brokerage conduct

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A broker, in an effort to win over a rival brokerage's prospective clients, tells those prospective clients false and damaging statements about the rival brokerage's business practices, knowing the statements are untrue. Beyond any license-law discipline, what separate civil business tort could this conduct implicate?
choice_a: Business disparagement/defamation -- knowingly making false, damaging statements about a competitor's business reputation can give rise to civil liability distinct from license-law discipline
choice_b: No civil tort could ever apply to statements made in a competitive business context, regardless of their truth or falsity
choice_c: This can only ever be pursued as a criminal antitrust matter, never as a civil claim
choice_d: This is protected, privileged speech under all circumstances because it was made in the course of soliciting business
explanation: Knowingly false and damaging statements made about a competitor's business (as distinct from honest, non-defamatory comparative statements) can support a civil business disparagement or defamation claim -- a separate exposure from DOS license discipline for untrustworthy conduct, illustrating that ethical and legal risk in competitive real estate practice extends beyond Article 12-A's own disciplinary framework.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general business-tort doctrine (business disparagement/defamation), applied to competitive real estate brokerage conduct
